Monte Carlo control

Lesson 37 measured a fixed policy. Control means finding a good one. Apply generalised policy iteration (Lesson 34) with Monte Carlo as the evaluation step: estimate action values from played hands, act greedily on them, repeat.

S&B Example 5.3: Monte Carlo with exploring starts. Each hand starts in a random state with a random first action, then follows the current greedy policy. It starts from "stick on 20 or 21". H hit, S stick. Amber outlines mark cells that differ from the exact optimal policy.

"Expected reward per hand" is exact: the greedy policy's value averaged over the initial deal, computed from the rules (the learner never sees this). The best possible is per hand. Some cells take millions of hands, such as hard 16 against a 10 and hard 12 against a 4, where hitting and sticking differ by less than 0.01.

Without exploring starts

Real hands start from the deal, not from a state you choose. The fix is to keep exploring: an ε-greedy policy (S&B §5.4) picks a random action with probability $\varepsilon = 0.1$. Both learners play 1,000,000 hands. The lines show the exact value of each one's greedy policy.

The maths

Without a model, $V$ is not enough to act on: choosing $\arg\max_a \sum p\,[r + \gamma V(s')]$ needs $p$. So Monte Carlo control estimates action values $Q(s, a)$ instead, by averaging the returns that followed each state–action pair:

$$Q(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t, A_t) + \frac{1}{N(S_t, A_t)}\big(G_t - Q(S_t, A_t)\big)$$

Then the policy improves greedily, with no model needed:

$$\pi(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s, a)$$

This is GPI with one episode of evaluation between improvements. Greedy with respect to $q_\pi$ is an improvement by Lesson 31's theorem.

The exploration problem. A greedy policy never tries the actions it thinks are worse, so their $Q$ never gets corrected. Exploring starts fixes this by starting each episode at a random state–action pair, so every pair is tried infinitely often.

ε-greedy fixes it without control over starts. With $|\mathcal{A}(s)|$ actions:

$$\pi(a \mid s) = \begin{cases} 1 - \varepsilon + \dfrac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal{A}(s)|} & a = \arg\max_{a'} Q(s, a') \\[2mm] \dfrac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal{A}(s)|} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Every action keeps probability at least $\varepsilon/|\mathcal{A}(s)|$. The policy improvement theorem still holds within the class of such policies, so this converges to the best ε-soft policy, not the best policy. Its greedy part is what the comparison plots.
